Title: City and County of Summit?
Chunks: 0,1
The City and County of Summit. It is an idea whose time has come. We’ve moved way beyond our town and resort boundaries. We are no longer small geographic areas. Nearly all of our population lives within a 10-mile radius.
I am not kidding. We could save millions of your hard-earned tax dollars by becoming the City and County of Summit.
Imagine: One police department instead of five. One water department instead of seven or eight. One wastewater department instead of more than I can think of. One fire department instead of four.
* * *
* * *
Millions of dollars are wasted on boards and administration – millions wasted just so communities can “have their own.”
A few months ago, I heard a report to the Breckenridge Town Council that said the economic viability of Main Street Breckenridge is directly connected to the economic viability of the Factory Outlet Stores in Silverthorne.
* * *
* * *
What more proof do we need to understand we are all in this thing together?
As Rodney King asked, “Why can’t we all just get along?”
First, we would have to win enabling legislation from the Colorado General Assembly to allow an election to abolish all the special districts, the towns and county government.
The same legislation would provide for the establishment of one city government headed by a mayor or chief executive and elected officials from each of the local communities. There would probably be seven, although any odd number would work.
Our current elected offices would cease to exist. The county clerk and recorder would become the city clerk; the treasurer and assessor would be folded into a finance department; the sheriff and coroner would be replaced by a department of public safety that also would include all of the fire, ambulance and emergency communication functions.
The surveyor – yes, that is an elected position – would be part of community development.
The county would be divided into communities.
As examples, we could have these communities: Heeney, Silverthorne-Dillon, Keystone, Montezuma, Frisco, Copper Mountain, Breckenridge and Blue River. All parts of the county would be in one of the communities.
This model works very well in Maryland, parts of Virginia, New Jersey, New York and Connecticut. In those areas they have a “county” government that provides all of the normal government services.
There are local communities whose representatives meet to discuss relevant planning and local issues.

Outside of Summit County, we already are viewed as “Summit County.” The town and resort lines disappear. Watch CNN or the Weather Channel as they talk about the weather or some event and the title at the bottom of the screen will say “Summit County, Colorado.” Yes, it might mention “Copper Mountain” or “Breckenridge,” but that is secondary.
Consider how important we would become in the eyes of resort communities. Eagle County is not Eagle County, but it is Vail. Pitkin County is not Pitkin County, but it is Aspen. Routt County is not Routt County, but it is Steamboat. San Miguel County is not San Miguel County, but it is Telluride.
This is not true in Summit County. Summit County is Summit County. It is not a particular resort. End of story.
I have lived in Summit County for almost 29 years. For almost that entire time, turf battles have erupted among towns over sales tax revenues. Battles occur each year to outspend and out-promote events in disregard for what would be good for the community as a whole.
We read recently about the continuing legal action resulting from the attempt to relocate Wal-Mart to Silverthorne. Dillon sold its soul to get City Market from Silverthorne a few years ago.
Now Silverthorne has hooked Target, and Frisco is gearing up to allow Wal-Mart to become a “super” Wal-Mart. When is this madness going to end?
I am here to tell you enough is enough. I think we have reached critical mass in our thinking about government.
This silly behavior on the part of our elected officials – and I am one – has to end. This competitive behavior only costs the taxpayers millions of dollars to the amusement of some elected officials. It is not their money to play with. It is time to insist we achieve efficiency in government.
Several of your elected officials have told me they support this idea, but I will let them speak for themselves.
I know this might not ever happen in my lifetime. I just think it is time for all of us to think outside the box. We must think about the future. Our future is going to be better and stronger if we are the City and County of Summit. Let the discussion begin.
————-
Columnist Gary Lindstrom, a county commissioner, can be found writing in this space on Thursdays.

Title: City and County of Summit?
Chunks: 0,1
The City and County of Summit. It is an idea whose time has come. We’ve moved way beyond our town and resort boundaries. We are no longer small geographic areas. Nearly all of our population lives within a 10-mile radius.
I am not kidding. We could save millions of your hard-earned tax dollars by becoming the City and County of Summit.
Imagine: One police department instead of five. One water department instead of seven or eight. One wastewater department instead of more than I can think of. One fire department instead of four.
* * *
* * *
Millions of dollars are wasted on boards and administration – millions wasted just so communities can “have their own.”
A few months ago, I heard a report to the Breckenridge Town Council that said the economic viability of Main Street Breckenridge is directly connected to the economic viability of the Factory Outlet Stores in Silverthorne.
* * *
* * *
What more proof do we need to understand we are all in this thing together?
As Rodney King asked, “Why can’t we all just get along?”
First, we would have to win enabling legislation from the Colorado General Assembly to allow an election to abolish all the special districts, the towns and county government.
The same legislation would provide for the establishment of one city government headed by a mayor or chief executive and elected officials from each of the local communities. There would probably be seven, although any odd number would work.
Our current elected offices would cease to exist. The county clerk and recorder would become the city clerk; the treasurer and assessor would be folded into a finance department; the sheriff and coroner would be replaced by a department of public safety that also would include all of the fire, ambulance and emergency communication functions.
The surveyor – yes, that is an elected position – would be part of community development.
The county would be divided into communities.
As examples, we could have these communities: Heeney, Silverthorne-Dillon, Keystone, Montezuma, Frisco, Copper Mountain, Breckenridge and Blue River. All parts of the county would be in one of the communities.
This model works very well in Maryland, parts of Virginia, New Jersey, New York and Connecticut. In those areas they have a “county” government that provides all of the normal government services.
There are local communities whose representatives meet to discuss relevant planning and local issues.

Outside of Summit County, we already are viewed as “Summit County.” The town and resort lines disappear. Watch CNN or the Weather Channel as they talk about the weather or some event and the title at the bottom of the screen will say “Summit County, Colorado.” Yes, it might mention “Copper Mountain” or “Breckenridge,” but that is secondary.
Consider how important we would become in the eyes of resort communities. Eagle County is not Eagle County, but it is Vail. Pitkin County is not Pitkin County, but it is Aspen. Routt County is not Routt County, but it is Steamboat. San Miguel County is not San Miguel County, but it is Telluride.
This is not true in Summit County. Summit County is Summit County. It is not a particular resort. End of story.
I have lived in Summit County for almost 29 years. For almost that entire time, turf battles have erupted among towns over sales tax revenues. Battles occur each year to outspend and out-promote events in disregard for what would be good for the community as a whole.
We read recently about the continuing legal action resulting from the attempt to relocate Wal-Mart to Silverthorne. Dillon sold its soul to get City Market from Silverthorne a few years ago.
Now Silverthorne has hooked Target, and Frisco is gearing up to allow Wal-Mart to become a “super” Wal-Mart. When is this madness going to end?
I am here to tell you enough is enough. I think we have reached critical mass in our thinking about government.
This silly behavior on the part of our elected officials – and I am one – has to end. This competitive behavior only costs the taxpayers millions of dollars to the amusement of some elected officials. It is not their money to play with. It is time to insist we achieve efficiency in government.
Several of your elected officials have told me they support this idea, but I will let them speak for themselves.
I know this might not ever happen in my lifetime. I just think it is time for all of us to think outside the box. We must think about the future. Our future is going to be better and stronger if we are the City and County of Summit. Let the discussion begin.
————-
Columnist Gary Lindstrom, a county commissioner, can be found writing in this space on Thursdays.

Title: Population of Summit County
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6
The population of Summit County and its towns rose and fell with the fortunes of mining.
From an initial estimate of “hundreds” in the county in 1860 during the first gold rush, the number dropped to 258 by 1870. With the second boom in 1880, the number of residents grew to 5459, only to drop to 1906 by 1890 because of the looming national silver crisis. Dredging operations and a revival of placer mining at the turn of the century brought the number to 2744 in the 1900 census.
Census date for Breckenridge show the same growth and decline pattern: a total of 51 in 1870; an increase in 1880 to 1657; a decline to 714 in 1890; and by 1900, a rise to 976.
Some in Breckenridge claimed northern European ancestry, but most were native-born. Of those residing in Breckenridge in 1870, 37 were born in the United States; 14 on foreign soil.
In Summit County in 1870, the native-born population arrived mainly from Ohio, New York and Pennsylvania. These same three states plus Illinois led the list in 1880. In 1885, those born in Colorado now outnumbered those born in Pennsylvania and elsewhere.
The foreign-born in Colorado in 1860 came from, in descending order, Canada, Ireland, the German states, England and Scotland. By the 1870 census, not much had changed. The Irish, escaping the potato famine, now ranked first; then the Germans, the English, and in fourth place, the Canadians. In 1880, the English took first place; then the Irish, Germans and Canadians in descending order. The German Empire by that time had united the German states, principalities and kingdoms. If Wales, Cornwall and England are considered as one along with Canada and Ireland, then these areas sent the greatest number of immigrants to Colorado in 1860, 1870 and 1880.

Breckenridge and Summit County followed national trends. Foreign-born residents in the county arrived mainly from northern Europe. The 1870 census listed 11 from British America (Canada), 28 from England and Wales; 14 from Ireland; three from Scotland; 27 from Germany; three from Norway and Sweden and two from Denmark.
Gold fever hit London hard, resulting in a large migration to Colorado. One writer called Colorado “England beyond the Missouri.”
In Cornwall, poor working conditions, starvation, low wages, poor management of the mines and growing unemployment pushed the Cornish miner to the US. First settling in the eastern states, the Cornish eventually brought their skills and expertise to Colorado and Summit County. The presence of certain social organizations and religious institutions tells of the Cornish who lived in Summit County: the Masons, Knight of Pythias, Independent Order of Odd Fellows, and, of course, the Methodist Church.
A substantial number of immigrants claimed Germany as “home.” Many arrived in Summit County with no plans to work in the mines. They felt that finding a stable economic future rested in applying a trade in places other than the mines. They became carpenters, saloon keepers, merchants or boardinghouse proprietors. So many Germans lived in Colorado that for 12 years (1877-1899), the state printed its laws in German as well as in English and Spanish. They did not abstain from card playing, dancing or drinking, even on Sundays–restrictions strictly observed by the Cornish Methodists.
Many residents perceived the Chinese as a threat to miners and merchants as well as to the general economic environment of the area. Thus they did not welcome the “Celestials.” The newspaper editor wrote that they would “drive out white labor, empty the schools, cause merchants to carry little variety and cheap goods, and make the efforts of the last 20-plus years meaningless. It would be better to let the placers lie idle than bring the Chinese to work them.” He editorialized, “Let those here stay but let no one else in.”
Chinese workers engaged in placer mining in French Gulch; on Barney Ford Hill at the head of Mayo and Illinois gulches, and south of Breckenridge, along the Blue River. In 1888, when Chinese arrived to work some placers near Lincoln, the newspaper editor commented that “Chinese were not required and none would be tolerated.”

Despite the animosity directed toward the Chinese, the Journal editor wrote about the Chinese New Year in very friendly terms, mentioning that Choy, who worked at the laundry, gave candies and nuts to the children in town.
No Chinese were counted in the Colorado census of 1860; the number grew to 7 in 1870.None lived in Summit County. By 1880, 601 lived in the state. All 19 in Summit County worked in laundries. Five years later, the number had grown to 21 in the county; 17 worked in placer mines; two worked as dishwashers and two worked in laundries.
As a rule, Chinese did not bring their families. Because Chinese women would not willing leave their homeland, researchers estimate that as many as 90 percent of the Chinese women in the United States were prostitutes. Many had been kidnapped or sold as indentured servants, sometimes even when still babies. Once in a mining town or camp, a Chinese woman had little opportunity to mix with other women in the community. Subject to the wishes of her husband, she spent her days doing laundry or sewing or ironing. Because Chinese men would not marry non-Chinese women, many prostitutes became wives to older Chinese men. In the 1880 Breckenridge census, one Chinese woman appears: Lee Cum, age 25, the wife of Lee Chun, age 52. Both worked in a laundry. Was she a prostitute who later became the wife of the much older man?
Those of Italian origin were no more welcome than the Chinese. The headlines screamed “Dealing in Dagoes — the Importation of 100 Organ Grinders Created Considerable Excitement” when the Pence-Miller Placer Company on the Blue River hired Italians to dig a ditch. Even after the turn of the century, some formal correspondence from county officials referred to Italians as “dagoes.”
Very few African-Americans lived in Summit County. The newspaper editor noted that so many “Darkies” worked placer mines in 1860 in Utah Gulch, one mile east of Breckenridge in French Gulch, that the gulch had been renamed for them. In 1885, the census counted five free African-Americans out of 258 county residents.

As would be expected of early mining towns with few amenities, young, unmarried males dominated.Those less bound by family and finances could more easily head west. Only later, as the towns grew, did females and children make up a larger portion of the population. In Summit County, between 1860 and 1885, unmarried single men composed the largest part of the population. Married men quite often came without their spouse or family. Generally, though, merchants and professionals brought their families. They expected to remain and build the town and economy rather than find their fortune and return “home.”
_written by Sandra F. Mather, PhD_

**Summit County** is a county located in the U.S. state of Colorado. As of the 2020 census, the population was 31,055,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-2020_Census_(City)-1) and was estimated to be 30,882 in 2024.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-QF-2) The county seat is Breckenridge.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-NACo-3) Summit County comprises the Breckenridge, CO Micropolitan Statistical Area.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-OMB_10-02-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-5)
Summit County was organized as one of the seventeen original Colorado counties by the First Territorial Legislature on November 1, 1861. It was named for the many mountain summits in the county. Until February 2, 1874, its boundaries included the area now comprising Summit County, Grand County, Routt County, Moffat County, Garfield County, Eagle County, and Rio Blanco County.
In 1874, the northern half of the original Summit County was split off to form Grand County; with the creation of Garfield and Eagle counties in 1883, Summit County arrived at its present boundaries. In addition, Summit County has seen two major boom eras.

According to the United States Census Bureau, the county has a total area of 619.259 square miles (1,603.87 km 2), of which 608.328 square miles (1,575.56 km 2) is land and 10.931 square miles (28.31 km 2) (1.77%) is water.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-6) It is the 55th largest county in Colorado by total area.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-7)
The terrain of the county is mountainous with elevations ranging from 7,957 feet (2,425 m) at Green Mountain Reservoir to 14,270 feet (4,350 m) at Grays Peak. The elevation of the county seat of Breckenridge is 9,602 feet (2,927 m), making it one of the highest cities in the state of Colorado and the United States.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-8) Much of the county has an alpine climate (ET in the Köppen Classification) characterized by tundra vegetation. Breckenridge and other similar elevations in the county have a subarctic climate (Dfc) characterized by cool summers and abundant snowfall in winter.

texts.0:
The population of Summit County and its towns rose and fell with the fortunes of mining.
From an initial estimate of “hundreds” in the county in 1860 during the first gold rush, the number dropped to 258 by 1870. With the second boom in 1880, the number of residents grew to 5459, only to drop to 1906 by 1890 because of the looming national silver crisis. Dredging operations and a revival of placer mining at the turn of the century brought the number to 2744 in the 1900 census.
Census date for Breckenridge show the same growth and decline pattern: a total of 51 in 1870; an increase in 1880 to 1657; a decline to 714 in 1890; and by 1900, a rise to 976.
Some in Breckenridge claimed northern European ancestry, but most were native-born. Of those residing in Breckenridge in 1870, 37 were born in the United States; 14 on foreign soil.
In Summit County in 1870, the native-born population arrived mainly from Ohio, New York and Pennsylvania. These same three states plus Illinois led the list in 1880. In 1885, those born in Colorado now outnumbered those born in Pennsylvania and elsewhere.
The foreign-born in Colorado in 1860 came from, in descending order, Canada, Ireland, the German states, England and Scotland. By the 1870 census, not much had changed. The Irish, escaping the potato famine, now ranked first; then the Germans, the English, and in fourth place, the Canadians. In 1880, the English took first place; then the Irish, Germans and Canadians in descending order. The German Empire by that time had united the German states, principalities and kingdoms. If Wales, Cornwall and England are considered as one along with Canada and Ireland, then these areas sent the greatest number of immigrants to Colorado in 1860, 1870 and 1880.
texts.1:
Breckenridge and Summit County followed national trends. Foreign-born residents in the county arrived mainly from northern Europe. The 1870 census listed 11 from British America (Canada), 28 from England and Wales; 14 from Ireland; three from Scotland; 27 from Germany; three from Norway and Sweden and two from Denmark.
Gold fever hit London hard, resulting in a large migration to Colorado. One writer called Colorado “England beyond the Missouri.”
In Cornwall, poor working conditions, starvation, low wages, poor management of the mines and growing unemployment pushed the Cornish miner to the US. First settling in the eastern states, the Cornish eventually brought their skills and expertise to Colorado and Summit County. The presence of certain social organizations and religious institutions tells of the Cornish who lived in Summit County: the Masons, Knight of Pythias, Independent Order of Odd Fellows, and, of course, the Methodist Church.
A substantial number of immigrants claimed Germany as “home.” Many arrived in Summit County with no plans to work in the mines. They felt that finding a stable economic future rested in applying a trade in places other than the mines. They became carpenters, saloon keepers, merchants or boardinghouse proprietors. So many Germans lived in Colorado that for 12 years (1877-1899), the state printed its laws in German as well as in English and Spanish. They did not abstain from card playing, dancing or drinking, even on Sundays–restrictions strictly observed by the Cornish Methodists.
Many residents perceived the Chinese as a threat to miners and merchants as well as to the general economic environment of the area. Thus they did not welcome the “Celestials.” The newspaper editor wrote that they would “drive out white labor, empty the schools, cause merchants to carry little variety and cheap goods, and make the efforts of the last 20-plus years meaningless. It would be better to let the placers lie idle than bring the Chinese to work them.” He editorialized, “Let those here stay but let no one else in.”
Chinese workers engaged in placer mining in French Gulch; on Barney Ford Hill at the head of Mayo and Illinois gulches, and south of Breckenridge, along the Blue River. In 1888, when Chinese arrived to work some placers near Lincoln, the newspaper editor commented that “Chinese were not required and none would be tolerated.”
texts.2:
Despite the animosity directed toward the Chinese, the Journal editor wrote about the Chinese New Year in very friendly terms, mentioning that Choy, who worked at the laundry, gave candies and nuts to the children in town.
No Chinese were counted in the Colorado census of 1860; the number grew to 7 in 1870.None lived in Summit County. By 1880, 601 lived in the state. All 19 in Summit County worked in laundries. Five years later, the number had grown to 21 in the county; 17 worked in placer mines; two worked as dishwashers and two worked in laundries.
As a rule, Chinese did not bring their families. Because Chinese women would not willing leave their homeland, researchers estimate that as many as 90 percent of the Chinese women in the United States were prostitutes. Many had been kidnapped or sold as indentured servants, sometimes even when still babies. Once in a mining town or camp, a Chinese woman had little opportunity to mix with other women in the community. Subject to the wishes of her husband, she spent her days doing laundry or sewing or ironing. Because Chinese men would not marry non-Chinese women, many prostitutes became wives to older Chinese men. In the 1880 Breckenridge census, one Chinese woman appears: Lee Cum, age 25, the wife of Lee Chun, age 52. Both worked in a laundry. Was she a prostitute who later became the wife of the much older man?
Those of Italian origin were no more welcome than the Chinese. The headlines screamed “Dealing in Dagoes — the Importation of 100 Organ Grinders Created Considerable Excitement” when the Pence-Miller Placer Company on the Blue River hired Italians to dig a ditch. Even after the turn of the century, some formal correspondence from county officials referred to Italians as “dagoes.”
Very few African-Americans lived in Summit County. The newspaper editor noted that so many “Darkies” worked placer mines in 1860 in Utah Gulch, one mile east of Breckenridge in French Gulch, that the gulch had been renamed for them. In 1885, the census counted five free African-Americans out of 258 county residents.
texts.3:
As would be expected of early mining towns with few amenities, young, unmarried males dominated.Those less bound by family and finances could more easily head west. Only later, as the towns grew, did females and children make up a larger portion of the population. In Summit County, between 1860 and 1885, unmarried single men composed the largest part of the population. Married men quite often came without their spouse or family. Generally, though, merchants and professionals brought their families. They expected to remain and build the town and economy rather than find their fortune and return “home.”
_written by Sandra F. Mather, PhD_

**Summit County** is a county located in the U.S. state of Colorado. As of the 2020 census, the population was 31,055,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-2020_Census_(City)-1) and was estimated to be 30,882 in 2024.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-QF-2) The county seat is Breckenridge.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-NACo-3) Summit County comprises the Breckenridge, CO Micropolitan Statistical Area.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-OMB_10-02-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-5)
Summit County was organized as one of the seventeen original Colorado counties by the First Territorial Legislature on November 1, 1861. It was named for the many mountain summits in the county. Until February 2, 1874, its boundaries included the area now comprising Summit County, Grand County, Routt County, Moffat County, Garfield County, Eagle County, and Rio Blanco County.
In 1874, the northern half of the original Summit County was split off to form Grand County; with the creation of Garfield and Eagle counties in 1883, Summit County arrived at its present boundaries. In addition, Summit County has seen two major boom eras.
texts.2:
According to the United States Census Bureau, the county has a total area of 619.259 square miles (1,603.87 km 2), of which 608.328 square miles (1,575.56 km 2) is land and 10.931 square miles (28.31 km 2) (1.77%) is water.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-6) It is the 55th largest county in Colorado by total area.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-7)
The terrain of the county is mountainous with elevations ranging from 7,957 feet (2,425 m) at Green Mountain Reservoir to 14,270 feet (4,350 m) at Grays Peak. The elevation of the county seat of Breckenridge is 9,602 feet (2,927 m), making it one of the highest cities in the state of Colorado and the United States.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-8) Much of the county has an alpine climate (ET in the Köppen Classification) characterized by tundra vegetation. Breckenridge and other similar elevations in the county have a subarctic climate (Dfc) characterized by cool summers and abundant snowfall in winter.

The population of Summit County and its towns rose and fell with the fortunes of mining.
From an initial estimate of “hundreds” in the county in 1860 during the first gold rush, the number dropped to 258 by 1870. With the second boom in 1880, the number of residents grew to 5459, only to drop to 1906 by 1890 because of the looming national silver crisis. Dredging operations and a revival of placer mining at the turn of the century brought the number to 2744 in the 1900 census.
Census date for Breckenridge show the same growth and decline pattern: a total of 51 in 1870; an increase in 1880 to 1657; a decline to 714 in 1890; and by 1900, a rise to 976.
Some in Breckenridge claimed northern European ancestry, but most were native-born. Of those residing in Breckenridge in 1870, 37 were born in the United States; 14 on foreign soil.
In Summit County in 1870, the native-born population arrived mainly from Ohio, New York and Pennsylvania. These same three states plus Illinois led the list in 1880. In 1885, those born in Colorado now outnumbered those born in Pennsylvania and elsewhere.
The foreign-born in Colorado in 1860 came from, in descending order, Canada, Ireland, the German states, England and Scotland. By the 1870 census, not much had changed. The Irish, escaping the potato famine, now ranked first; then the Germans, the English, and in fourth place, the Canadians. In 1880, the English took first place; then the Irish, Germans and Canadians in descending order. The German Empire by that time had united the German states, principalities and kingdoms. If Wales, Cornwall and England are considered as one along with Canada and Ireland, then these areas sent the greatest number of immigrants to Colorado in 1860, 1870 and 1880.

Breckenridge and Summit County followed national trends. Foreign-born residents in the county arrived mainly from northern Europe. The 1870 census listed 11 from British America (Canada), 28 from England and Wales; 14 from Ireland; three from Scotland; 27 from Germany; three from Norway and Sweden and two from Denmark.
Gold fever hit London hard, resulting in a large migration to Colorado. One writer called Colorado “England beyond the Missouri.”
In Cornwall, poor working conditions, starvation, low wages, poor management of the mines and growing unemployment pushed the Cornish miner to the US. First settling in the eastern states, the Cornish eventually brought their skills and expertise to Colorado and Summit County. The presence of certain social organizations and religious institutions tells of the Cornish who lived in Summit County: the Masons, Knight of Pythias, Independent Order of Odd Fellows, and, of course, the Methodist Church.
A substantial number of immigrants claimed Germany as “home.” Many arrived in Summit County with no plans to work in the mines. They felt that finding a stable economic future rested in applying a trade in places other than the mines. They became carpenters, saloon keepers, merchants or boardinghouse proprietors. So many Germans lived in Colorado that for 12 years (1877-1899), the state printed its laws in German as well as in English and Spanish. They did not abstain from card playing, dancing or drinking, even on Sundays–restrictions strictly observed by the Cornish Methodists.
Many residents perceived the Chinese as a threat to miners and merchants as well as to the general economic environment of the area. Thus they did not welcome the “Celestials.” The newspaper editor wrote that they would “drive out white labor, empty the schools, cause merchants to carry little variety and cheap goods, and make the efforts of the last 20-plus years meaningless. It would be better to let the placers lie idle than bring the Chinese to work them.” He editorialized, “Let those here stay but let no one else in.”
Chinese workers engaged in placer mining in French Gulch; on Barney Ford Hill at the head of Mayo and Illinois gulches, and south of Breckenridge, along the Blue River. In 1888, when Chinese arrived to work some placers near Lincoln, the newspaper editor commented that “Chinese were not required and none would be tolerated.”

Despite the animosity directed toward the Chinese, the Journal editor wrote about the Chinese New Year in very friendly terms, mentioning that Choy, who worked at the laundry, gave candies and nuts to the children in town.
No Chinese were counted in the Colorado census of 1860; the number grew to 7 in 1870.None lived in Summit County. By 1880, 601 lived in the state. All 19 in Summit County worked in laundries. Five years later, the number had grown to 21 in the county; 17 worked in placer mines; two worked as dishwashers and two worked in laundries.
As a rule, Chinese did not bring their families. Because Chinese women would not willing leave their homeland, researchers estimate that as many as 90 percent of the Chinese women in the United States were prostitutes. Many had been kidnapped or sold as indentured servants, sometimes even when still babies. Once in a mining town or camp, a Chinese woman had little opportunity to mix with other women in the community. Subject to the wishes of her husband, she spent her days doing laundry or sewing or ironing. Because Chinese men would not marry non-Chinese women, many prostitutes became wives to older Chinese men. In the 1880 Breckenridge census, one Chinese woman appears: Lee Cum, age 25, the wife of Lee Chun, age 52. Both worked in a laundry. Was she a prostitute who later became the wife of the much older man?
Those of Italian origin were no more welcome than the Chinese. The headlines screamed “Dealing in Dagoes — the Importation of 100 Organ Grinders Created Considerable Excitement” when the Pence-Miller Placer Company on the Blue River hired Italians to dig a ditch. Even after the turn of the century, some formal correspondence from county officials referred to Italians as “dagoes.”
Very few African-Americans lived in Summit County. The newspaper editor noted that so many “Darkies” worked placer mines in 1860 in Utah Gulch, one mile east of Breckenridge in French Gulch, that the gulch had been renamed for them. In 1885, the census counted five free African-Americans out of 258 county residents.

As would be expected of early mining towns with few amenities, young, unmarried males dominated.Those less bound by family and finances could more easily head west. Only later, as the towns grew, did females and children make up a larger portion of the population. In Summit County, between 1860 and 1885, unmarried single men composed the largest part of the population. Married men quite often came without their spouse or family. Generally, though, merchants and professionals brought their families. They expected to remain and build the town and economy rather than find their fortune and return “home.”

**Summit County** is a county located in the U.S. state of Colorado. As of the 2020 census, the population was 31,055,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-2020_Census_(City)-1) and was estimated to be 30,882 in 2024.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-QF-2) The county seat is Breckenridge.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-NACo-3) Summit County comprises the Breckenridge, CO Micropolitan Statistical Area.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-OMB_10-02-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-5)
Summit County was organized as one of the seventeen original Colorado counties by the First Territorial Legislature on November 1, 1861. It was named for the many mountain summits in the county. Until February 2, 1874, its boundaries included the area now comprising Summit County, Grand County, Routt County, Moffat County, Garfield County, Eagle County, and Rio Blanco County.
In 1874, the northern half of the original Summit County was split off to form Grand County; with the creation of Garfield and Eagle counties in 1883, Summit County arrived at its present boundaries. In addition, Summit County has seen two major boom eras.

According to the United States Census Bureau, the county has a total area of 619.259 square miles (1,603.87 km 2), of which 608.328 square miles (1,575.56 km 2) is land and 10.931 square miles (28.31 km 2) (1.77%) is water.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-6) It is the 55th largest county in Colorado by total area.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-7)
The terrain of the county is mountainous with elevations ranging from 7,957 feet (2,425 m) at Green Mountain Reservoir to 14,270 feet (4,350 m) at Grays Peak. The elevation of the county seat of Breckenridge is 9,602 feet (2,927 m), making it one of the highest cities in the state of Colorado and the United States.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Colorado#cite_note-8) Much of the county has an alpine climate (ET in the Köppen Classification) characterized by tundra vegetation. Breckenridge and other similar elevations in the county have a subarctic climate (Dfc) characterized by cool summers and abundant snowfall in winter.

## WELCOME TO SUMMIT, NEW JERSEY
_**Stylish refinement in a suburban community that offers it all**_
Located in Union County, Summit espouses an unmatched sense of style and refinement. With a population of 21,913, this quaint community is one of the closest New Jersey suburbs to both New York City and Newark. New York City is just 23 miles away, while Newark is a quick 12-mile drive. Whether you’re a commuter or just want to be close to city life, Summit is an ideal choice.
Aside from its fantastic location, this town is home to outstanding schools, abundant green space, tranquil neighborhoods, close-by shopping and dining, and plenty of area attractions. No matter who you are or how you enjoy spending your time, you’ll love living in Summit, New Jersey.
Prospective buyers will be thrilled to discover the large selection of opulent and spacious homes. Those seeking to purchase what could easily be deemed a luxurious dream property will find exactly what they are looking for. Currently, the median list price of homes in Summit sits just under $1 million.

## WHAT TO LOVE
*   Highly-rated schools  
*   Grand, stately homes and peaceful neighborhoods  
*   Many stunning green spaces to enjoy nature

## PEOPLE & LIFESTYLE
The overall feel in Summit can most accurately be described as refined, stylish, and suburban. Immaculate lawns and landscaping, stately homes, and quiet residential neighborhoods make the town a serene escape from the busyness of city life. The area is picturesque and ideal for anyone who enjoys the good things in life.
Summit is also a wonderful place to relocate for those who want to live close to either New York City or Newark, but who want to take life at a more relaxed pace. You can genuinely have the best of both city life and suburban comforts while living here.

## DINING, ENTERTAINMENT & SHOPPING
Shopping and dining in Summit is a treat. Locals are surrounded by top-tier restaurants and upscale stores that are a delight to frequent.
When planning a day of in-town shopping, you’ll have plenty of places to choose from. Along (and just off of) Springfield Avenue, plan a visit to theSummit Farmers Market, West Elm, lululemon athletica,Hilltop Bicycles,The Collective,Serena & Lily, Willow St., Apricot Lane Boutique, The Shade Store, and Wool & Grace.
Top-rated dining abounds throughout all of Summit. Whether you’re planning on grabbing a tasty meal for breakfast, lunch, or dinner, you’ll have no trouble finding something extraordinary to eat. Locals are a fan of places such asThe Committed Pig,Bonji Bowls,Barbacoa, Tito’s Burritos & Wings Summit,Natale’s Summit Bakery, and Roots Steakhouse.

## THINGS TO DO
Year-round, there is an almost never-ending list of options of things to see and do around Summit. From exclusive clubs to beautiful green spaces, residents don’t have to travel far to have a good time.
Looking to join an exceptional country club upon relocating to the area? At the Beacon Hill Club, you have the opportunity to enjoy abundant views and luxurious interior design, racquet sports, aquatics, and even ice sports. You can also explore the many wonderful amenities at the Canoe Brook Country Club.
Around (and just outside of) town, be sure to check out other area highlights. Top places to visit include theReeves-Reed Arboretum, Hidden Valley Park, Union County Open Space & Recreation Park, the Summit Historical Society,The Gravity Vault, Edison Recreation Center, and Summit Line Park.

## SCHOOLS
Summit is home to several excellent schools. Top educational opportunities include:
*   Lincoln Hubbard Elementary School, 1-5  
*   Franklin Elementary School, 1-5  
*   Summit Sr High School, 9-12

Climateedit
Summit has warm, humid summers and cold winters typical of northern New Jersey. July is the warmest month, with average high temperatures around 84°F (29°C) and lows near 69°F (21°C), while January is the coldest, with highs around 38°F (3°C) and lows near 25°F (−4°C). The city receives approximately 45 inches (1,150 mm) of precipitation a year, distributed fairly evenly across the seasons, along with an estimated 44 inches (112 cm) of snow in a typical winter, most of which falls in January and February.[56]

## WELCOME TO SUMMIT, NEW JERSEY
_**Stylish refinement in a suburban community that offers it all**_
Located in Union County, Summit espouses an unmatched sense of style and refinement. With a population of 21,913, this quaint community is one of the closest New Jersey suburbs to both New York City and Newark. New York City is just 23 miles away, while Newark is a quick 12-mile drive. Whether you’re a commuter or just want to be close to city life, Summit is an ideal choice.
Aside from its fantastic location, this town is home to outstanding schools, abundant green space, tranquil neighborhoods, close-by shopping and dining, and plenty of area attractions. No matter who you are or how you enjoy spending your time, you’ll love living in Summit, New Jersey.
Prospective buyers will be thrilled to discover the large selection of opulent and spacious homes. Those seeking to purchase what could easily be deemed a luxurious dream property will find exactly what they are looking for. Currently, the median list price of homes in Summit sits just under $1 million.

## WHAT TO LOVE
*   Highly-rated schools  
*   Grand, stately homes and peaceful neighborhoods  
*   Many stunning green spaces to enjoy nature

## PEOPLE & LIFESTYLE
The overall feel in Summit can most accurately be described as refined, stylish, and suburban. Immaculate lawns and landscaping, stately homes, and quiet residential neighborhoods make the town a serene escape from the busyness of city life. The area is picturesque and ideal for anyone who enjoys the good things in life.
Summit is also a wonderful place to relocate for those who want to live close to either New York City or Newark, but who want to take life at a more relaxed pace. You can genuinely have the best of both city life and suburban comforts while living here.

## DINING, ENTERTAINMENT & SHOPPING
Shopping and dining in Summit is a treat. Locals are surrounded by top-tier restaurants and upscale stores that are a delight to frequent.
When planning a day of in-town shopping, you’ll have plenty of places to choose from. Along (and just off of) Springfield Avenue, plan a visit to theSummit Farmers Market, West Elm, lululemon athletica,Hilltop Bicycles,The Collective,Serena & Lily, Willow St., Apricot Lane Boutique, The Shade Store, and Wool & Grace.
Top-rated dining abounds throughout all of Summit. Whether you’re planning on grabbing a tasty meal for breakfast, lunch, or dinner, you’ll have no trouble finding something extraordinary to eat. Locals are a fan of places such asThe Committed Pig,Bonji Bowls,Barbacoa, Tito’s Burritos & Wings Summit,Natale’s Summit Bakery, and Roots Steakhouse.

## THINGS TO DO
Year-round, there is an almost never-ending list of options of things to see and do around Summit. From exclusive clubs to beautiful green spaces, residents don’t have to travel far to have a good time.
Looking to join an exceptional country club upon relocating to the area? At the Beacon Hill Club, you have the opportunity to enjoy abundant views and luxurious interior design, racquet sports, aquatics, and even ice sports. You can also explore the many wonderful amenities at the Canoe Brook Country Club.
Around (and just outside of) town, be sure to check out other area highlights. Top places to visit include theReeves-Reed Arboretum, Hidden Valley Park, Union County Open Space & Recreation Park, the Summit Historical Society,The Gravity Vault, Edison Recreation Center, and Summit Line Park.
